title: Performance of Krotov, PRONTO and PINN for optimal control of quantum gates
authors: Martín D. Jiménez, Murilo D. Forlevesi, Emanuel F. de Lima, Leonardo K. Castelano
abstract: Achieving scalable quantum computing demands high-fidelity operations capable of mitigating population leakage into non-computational states. Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs) have recently emerged as a powerful paradigm to unify quantum hardware characterization (inverse problems) and pulse engineering (direct problems), laying the foundational architecture for autonomous quantum processors. However, standard PINN frameworks face severe numerical bottlenecks, such as spectral bias, when attempting to simultaneously solve highly oscillatory multi-level dynamics and optimize continuous control fields under strict global phase constraints. In this work, we propose an enhanced PINN scheme for quantum optimal control (PINNQOC) that circumvents these limitations by incorporating Fourier feature embeddings, dynamic epoch normalization, and an informed pre-training routine. To rigorously evaluate its performance, we systematically benchmark our framework against two premier continuous control solvers: the first-order Krotov method and the second-order Projection Operator Newton Method for Trajectory Optimization (PRONTO). These techniques are applied to implement multiple quantum gates on a truncated three-level fluxonium qubit and a four-level Nitrogen-Vacancy center coupled to a Carbon-13 nuclear spin. Our advanced PINNQOC approach successfully suppresses population leakage while achieving gate fidelities exceeding 99.9$\%$, matching the efficacy of traditional solvers. Finally, we provide a comprehensive analysis of computational times, iteration efficiency, and mean leakage, highlighting the distinct trade-offs and avenues for embedding physics-guided machine learning into automated quantum hardware pipelines.
summary: This paper develops an enhanced Physics-Informed Neural Network scheme (PINNQOC) for solving quantum optimal control problems. It benchmarks this ML approach against established methods like Krotov's and PRONTO's on multi-level qubit systems. The results show that PINNQOC achieves high fidelity while offering a promising pathway for real-time, adaptive control in future autonomous quantum hardware.
main_problem: The core problem is achieving high-fidelity quantum gate operations while actively suppressing population leakage into non-computational states.
main_result: The proposed PINNQOC framework successfully matches the fidelity of traditional solvers (Krotov, PRONTO) and demonstrates superior leakage suppression in multi-level systems.
method: The authors propose an enhanced Physics-Informed Neural Network scheme (PINNQOC) to solve quantum optimal control problems, benchmarking it against established gradient-based methods like Krotov's and PRONTO's optimization techniques.
model_or_system: The study uses truncated multi-level systems as models, specifically a three-level fluxonium qubit and a four-level Nitrogen-Vacancy center coupled to a Carbon-13 nuclear spin. The dynamics are governed by the time-dependent Schrödinger equation.
key_observables: Gate fidelity (target vs. achieved), mean population leakage ($\ell$), computational time, and iteration efficiency.
important_parameters: Penalization factors ($q=0.2$ or $0.3$), target gate specifications, and the number of time steps ($N_t$).
main_assumptions: Standard PINNs suffer from numerical bottlenecks (spectral bias) when solving highly oscillatory dynamics; traditional solvers are strictly trajectory-specific.
figures_summary: The notes indicate comparisons across multiple tables summarizing performance metrics for different gate types and system sizes, comparing fidelity, leakage, time, and iterations for the three methods.
paper_structure: The paper introduces the problem of high-fidelity control, details the theoretical background of QOC (Krotov/PRONTO), presents the novel PINNQOC framework enhancements, benchmarks performance on specific multi-level qubits, and concludes with an analysis of computational trade-offs for autonomous quantum hardware.
why_interesting: This work directly addresses the practical implementation challenges in quantum computing by providing a machine learning approach (PINN) that can automate pulse engineering and adapt to hardware imperfections better than purely analytical or trajectory-dependent solvers.
